maths_errors.text: co-interior angles (same side of the transversal, making a C-shape) add to 180°
maths_errors.correction: Being on the same side of the transversal is not enough. Corresponding angles are also on the same side, and they are equal, not supplementary. Co-interior angles are on the same side of the transversal AND both between the parallel lines. Only then do they add to 180°.

maths_errors.text: alternate angles (opposite sides of the transversal, making a Z-shape) are equal
maths_errors.correction: Being on opposite sides of the transversal is not enough. Many pairs of angles on opposite sides are not equal: one acute and one obtuse angle at different crossings add to 180°. Alternate angles are on opposite sides of the transversal AND both between the parallel lines, one at each crossing.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only states 'Angles in a triangle = 180°'. It never derives it, for example by drawing a line parallel to one side and using alternate angles. This is despite the title 'Angles — rules and proofs'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (eg to deduce and use the angle sum in any polygon, and to derive properties of regular polygons)
missing_spec_content.why: Only the quadrilateral sum is given ('Angles in a quadrilateral = 360°'), with no reason. The lesson does not cover: the polygon angle sum (n − 2) × 180°, splitting a polygon into triangles, exterior angles of polygons summing to 360°, or interior and exterior angles of regular polygons.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: colloquial terms such as Z angles are not acceptable and should not be used.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson pairs every parallel-line rule with 'F-shape', 'Z-shape', 'C-shape' (slides[1].formula, keyFacts[1]). It never warns that these terms will not earn the reason mark. slides[3].mistakes[0].correction even says 'Draw the letter in the diagram'. The student must be told to write 'alternate', 'corresponding' and 'co-interior' in reasons.

density.text: Angles on a straight line sum to 180° — they form a half-turn. Angles around a full point sum to 360° — a complete turn. The interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°; for a quadrilateral, 360°. Parallel-line rules: corresponding angles (same position at each crossing, making an F-shape) are equal; alternate angles (opposite sides of the transversal, making a Z-shape) are equal; co-interior angles (same side of the transversal, making a C-shape) add to 180°.
density.why: Seven rules in one paragraph. The last sentence carries three definitions with nested brackets. 'Transversal' is used without ever being defined.

density.text: Angles on a straight line = 180° | Angles around a point = 360° | Angles in a triangle = 180° | Angles in a quadrilateral = 360° | Corresponding angles (F-shape) are equal | Alternate angles (Z-shape) are equal | Co-interior angles (C-shape) add to 180°
density.why: Seven facts run together on one line separated by pipes, with no diagram for any of them.

density.text: When a line crosses two parallel lines it creates pairs of angles with special relationships — knowing those relationships lets you find any missing angle in a diagram without measuring.
density.why: One sentence carries several ideas: transversal, angle pairs, and solving without measuring. It names no relationship, and the earlier sentence already packs in three separate rules.

density.text: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle formed is 68°. Find the co-interior angle on the same side of the transversal.
density.why: There is no diagram, and the question never says the 68° angle lies between the parallel lines. Step 1 simply asserts 'The two angles are on the same side of the transversal between the parallel lines'. A first-time learner cannot see where the angles are or why they are co-interior.

density.text: The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
density.why: 'Exterior angle' and 'opposite interior angles' are never defined or shown, and the lesson gives no reason why the fact is true.

density.text: Co-interior angles (C-shape, also called allied or same-side interior) add to 180°.
density.why: This brings in three extra names for one idea inside a bracket, in the middle of a correction.

not_checked: The lesson contains no diagrams, so it is not possible to check that the 68° angle in slides[2] is positioned between the parallel lines as step 1 assumes.
